value.case: The account's limits are below what one endpoint needs
value.text: (two warning lines before the result, for an account that allows 5 streams and 100 MiB of disk: "warning: the account allows 5 streams; one endpoint needs 6, one more each" and "warning: the account has 100MiB of disk; one endpoint needs 109MiB"; an account that allows 6 streams and 109 MiB gets neither)
value.note: One endpoint needs the 5 buckets init makes plus its inbox stream, one consumer, and the buckets' caps (93 MiB with the defaults) plus the inbox cap (16 MiB) of disk, the numbers of docs/nats-server.md, Sizing, which also says one more stream and one more inbox cap are needed per further endpoint (the warning lines give only the numbers and keep to 80 columns). The warnings follow the limits in config.json; on a re-init a bucket whose cap was raised earlier counts at its live cap. A case in round brackets is a description: the conformance test skips it. The unit test TestLimitWarnings in cmd/mashctl checks the lines.

value.case: A strict operator and no signing_key
value.text: warning: no signing_key in mash-setup.yaml; this server may require one
value.note: The condition, in plain words: the account lists signing keys, the setup file has no signing_key, and no signing key is already stored. In that case the warning appears (and no signing key is already stored). One line before the result; exit stays 0 and the setup goes on; printed once. init does not read the operator's JWT, so it cannot see strict_signing_key_usage: listed signing keys are the only sign it has that the operator will require one. Applies to init only.

value.note: With a signing_key set, init writes nothing to stderr. A case in round brackets is a description: the conformance test skips it; init_signing_warn_test.go checks it.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, this job was done by mashctl adopt, mashctl init and mashctl init --local. mashctl does not install or start NATS; the NATS quick-start script writes this file as its last step.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: Safe to run again with the same settings. It never replaces what a folder already holds: if the folder was set up with a different operator key, account key, server, system creds, admin creds, signing key or owner, it refuses and changes nothing, in one line of the same form naming which ('... was set up with a different owner; nothing was changed'), and the way on is a new configuration folder (--config-dir) or moving the old folder aside yourself. Someone who removes a script-made server and sets one up again meets this every time; it is a known issue for 0.5.6 with that workaround. THE SETUP FILE is YAML, and holds paths, never secrets: 'servers' (a list of addresses), 'ca' (the certificate authority's certificate, if the server uses its own), 'owner' (the first owner), 'admin_creds' (the administrator's creds file), 'system_creds' (the system account's creds file), 'operator_key' (the operator key that signs the account: its identity key when the server was set up with the nats command, or a signing key if your operator uses one), 'account_key' (the account's identity key) and, optionally, 'signing_key' (one of the account's signing seeds, a 0600 file: when set, endpoint users are signed with it, which a strict operator needs; init refuses a key that is not listed in the account JWT, is the identity key or is scoped; the default result does not show the key: --detail adds a line, 'Signing key: ' and its public key (69 columns), and --json has it as signing_key_pub; init also records its public key, never the seed, in config.json as signing_key_pub, so that when both signing.nk and signing.pub are later lost mashctl refuses to create endpoints and names mashctl init instead of signing with the identity key). If the folder was set up with a different signing key, init refuses the same way. The operator and account keys are what cancelling a deleted endpoint's key needs. Know what this means: with a server set up by the script, mashctl's folder holds the operator's identity key, the strongest key there is, with which the operator itself can be re-issued. It is protected only as your own files are. A hosted NATS where you do not hold the operator key, such as Synadia Cloud, is not supported by mashctl in 0.5.6; mash itself works against any conforming server.

value.why: Administration. There are no MCP tools for mashctl.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, these checks were mashctl audit and mashctl issued check. mashctl issued list has no command of its own any more: one endpoint's issue record is in mashctl endpoint show.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: What is a warning and what is a problem. Warnings: a lease with no endpoint, a retired name seen in use, and a missing record store (issued, adoption or retired) on the storage row; the fix for a missing store is to run mashctl init --config <file> again, which is safe. A missing issue store also fails the keys row (no issue record; mashctl cannot tell its users from others), with or without --audit-users. A problem: an endpoint whose credentials were being cancelled and never finished; the fix is to run that mashctl endpoint delete again.

value.note: One line is added: the next step, a command to run as printed. Today: the first two lines. With no --out the creds are installed on this machine, so the endpoint can run here at once (docs/operations.md, Adding an endpoint). What a person does with a new endpoint is start a session as it: docs/guide/by-hand.md step 6 (MASH_ENDPOINT=acme.demo.bob claude), docs/install.md section 5 (Launch a session) and the setup skill's last steps (it writes a one-word launcher with the same MASH_ENDPOINT export). The setup skill also checks MASH_ENDPOINT=acme.demo.bob mash status first (it expects ready, offline); that is a check, not a use, so it is not the line. The line is not printed for --out (the join file is for another machine, where mash join <file> is the step; a case for it can follow) or for --dry-run. The one-line rule "An action prints one line" allows the file location; this is a second addition and is for the lead to rule on.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, this was also reachable as deprovision, which is removed. Typing the name to confirm is what gh repo delete does.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: Order. The endpoint's key is cancelled on every server first; only when every server confirms is anything removed, so a failure there leaves the endpoint whole. If this machine holds the endpoint's creds file, it is set aside as <address>.creds.deleted, a marker that keeps the endpoint's name and its JWT only, no key, so mash no longer counts it as installed; the path is predictable and nothing prints it. Nothing else on any machine is touched. If a step after the cancellation fails, the error is one line naming the address and the cause in plain words, with the command to run again; the key is already cancelled, so its credentials no longer work, and running the command again is safe.

7       alice  1m ago  verified  yes        task  48 B

value.note: TO-6, REQ-006, CHG-9. The header counts only the messages mashctl itself finds malformed (a header fault), and says what it counts (ADR 0174, planner #3665); a message that was not verified is not in it. The endpoint's own count (`mash inbox`, `mash status --detail`) can be higher, because it also refuses mail it could not verify, by its own setting. The refused messages are among the not-delivered ones. TRUST is `refused` where 0.5.9 printed `forged` for a message with a header fault, and the class is the REASON. A message that was not verified keeps its trust label and gets `not verified` as its REASON. The REASON column is the last cell and the only one cut, with `…` at 79 columns, as a preview is, and is named in the header only when some message has one. `--json` carries the whole class.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, this was mashctl inbox inspect, with --from and --to. Those are replaced by --after, the option mash inbox has.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: An administrator sees everything stored. FROM is the address a message claims, and '?' when it names no sender at all (the same '?' in the JSON); messages are delivered in order, so a delivered message never follows an undelivered one; TRUST says whether that claim was proven, in mash's own labels: verified, unknown-signer, claimed, absent, stale, forged or refused. `refused` is a message with a header fault: its REASON is the class (the same words as mash inbox shows), and the JSON has the same class as 'reason', present on a refused message and on a message that was not verified, absent on the others. 'refused' in the JSON object counts the messages mashctl itself finds malformed that are still in the stream, as the header does; a message that was not verified is not in it, keeps its trust label and gets `not verified` as its reason. DELIVERED is yes or no, and means only that the endpoint took the message off the server. Whether the endpoint then showed it or refused it is decided on the endpoint's own machine and is not something mashctl can see: by default an endpoint refuses everything that is not verified, so a 'yes' beside any other trust label most likely means it was refused. In --json, `when` is the time the message was stored, in RFC 3339 and UTC, with a fraction of a second when the server stored one (for example 2026-11-26T15:04:05Z or 2026-11-26T15:04:05.12Z).

value.text:
Usage: mashctl <verb> [args]

An endpoint is one agent's mailbox, addressed owner.group.name; the owner, the
first part, is the account that holds it. SAP is the Synadia Agent Protocol,
NATS is the message server mash talks to, creds are the file that signs an
endpoint in to it, and a trust label ([verified] and the others) says whether a
message's sender is proven.

  mashctl init --config path [--dry-run] [--json]
      set mash up on a NATS server you already have, from a setup file; safe to
      run again
  mashctl status [--json]
      one line per server: whether it works, how many endpoints it has, how many
      are online
  mashctl limits show [--json]
      print the limits in force
  mashctl doctor [--strict] [--json]
      check the server, mash's storage on it and every endpoint's records, and
      say how to fix what is wrong; changes nothing
  mashctl limits apply [prefix] [--dry-run] [--json]
      raise existing inboxes to the configured limits (never lowers); prefix is
      an owner, owner.group or one address
  mashctl endpoint list [prefix] [--wide] [--json]
      the endpoints in the directory
  mashctl endpoint show <address> [--json]
      one endpoint: its state, labels and public key
  mashctl endpoint create <address> [--out PATH] [--public-key PATH] [--dry-run]
          [--json]
      make an endpoint and its credentials, for example acme.demo.bob
  mashctl endpoint reissue <address> [--out PATH] [--public-key PATH]
          [--dry-run] [--json]
      give an endpoint new credentials and cancel the old ones
  mashctl endpoint delete <address> [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]
      revoke the endpoint's user key, remove its record and inbox, burn the
      address, rename its creds file
  mashctl endpoint set <address> key=value... [--dry-run] [--json]
      set role, description, host, capability or label.NAME
  mashctl endpoint unset <address> key... [--dry-run] [--json]
      remove those values
  mashctl endpoint suspend <address> [--json]
      refuse new mail to an endpoint; its stored mail and credentials stay
  mashctl endpoint resume <address> [--json]
      take new mail again, undoing suspend
  mashctl endpoint inbox <address> [--after number] [--limit n] [--json]
      what is in an endpoint's inbox, without any message text
  mashctl endpoint permissions <address> [--json]
      the NATS permissions an endpoint's user needs
  mashctl version [--json]
      print the version and the commit

Global options (before or after the verb):
  --server <url>       The server address. May be given more than once.
  --creds <path>       The administrator's creds file.
  --ca <path>          The certificate authority's certificate, when the server
                       uses its own.
  --config-dir <path>  The configuration folder. Default: ~/.config/mash.
  --detail             Print the fuller answer: after the usual line, more as
                       'label: value' lines; with --json, the fuller object.
  --json               Print the result as JSON.
  --no-color           Never use color.
  -h, --help           Show help for the command.

Run mashctl <command> --help for a command's options.
value.note: help-mashctl-top's planned text with three changes and nothing else. (1) usage: becomes Usage: (capital U, as mash). (2) ADDRESS becomes <address> in every verb line, as mash writes it; the create and reissue synopses are the 80-column wrap with the longer word (create still fits on one line, reissue wraps the same way). (3) One footer as the last line after a blank line: Run mashctl <command> --help for a command's options. Today: usage: mashctl <verb> [args], ADDRESS, no footer. Other placeholders (prefix, path, number, n) are not changed here. help-mashctl-top-usage-footer with the same glossary sentence as mash --help (the rule says the sentence is one, in the top-level help of both tools). "mash talks to" is as in mash's text: mashctl's own server is the same NATS server.
